paragraphs.source_en: Kangetsu said, “Then the haiku poet Takahama Kyoshi enters along the hanamichi, carrying a stick, wearing a white rush-stuffed hat, a gossamer haori, his Satsuma-patterned kimono tucked up, and low leather shoes on his feet. His costume looks somewhat like that of an army contractor, but since he is a haiku poet he must walk as leisurely as possible, with the air of being wholly absorbed in composing a verse within. Thus Kyoshi comes down the hanamichi and reaches the main stage; suddenly he raises his haiku-brooding eyes and sees before him a great willow tree, and beneath its shade a snow-white naked woman bathing. Startled, he looks up, and there on a long willow branch sits a crow, looking down at the woman as she bathes. At this, Master Kyoshi is deeply moved and the spirit of haiku wells up in him. This tableau should be held for about fifty seconds; then he chants a haiku aloud: ‘Ah, the crow / Enraptured by the woman / Bathing below.’ The moment the chant is finished, the clappers sound and the curtain falls. How is that? Is it not a novel idea? Does the play please you? It would be far more amusing for you to play Kyoshi than to take the role of Miss Omiya.”

paragraphs.source_zh: 寒月说：“就这样，俳人高滨虚子手执司的克，戴着白灯心草的帽子，穿着羽纱的外褂，把萨摩条纹布的长袍掖起，脚下一双矮腰皮鞋，从花道登场。他的这身穿戴，虽然有点像陆军部的御用商人，但因为是俳人，所以必须尽可能走得从容不迫，做出一副边走边在心里推敲着俳句创作的样子。这样，虚子穿过花道，来到舞台上，他突然抬起他那正在揣摩俳句的眼睛一看，面前是一棵大柳树，柳荫下一个雪白裸身的女子正在沐浴。他吃了一惊，往上一看，在长长的柳枝上停留着一只乌鸦正往下瞧着女人沐浴。于是虚子先生深有感触，俳兴大发。这个镜头大约需要保持五十秒钟，然后他大声朗吟了一首俳句：‘对沐浴的女人／看得神魂颠倒的／这只乌鸦哟。’一旦朗吟完毕，立刻响起拍子木，幕落。怎么样？这很有新意吧？你喜欢这个剧吗？你扮演虚子比起担当阿宫姑娘的角色来，要有意思得多哩。”

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei, who until then had been listening with comparative meekness, was not the sort of man who could remain silent forever. He said, “If that is all the plot there is, your haiku-drama is rather appalling. According to Mr. Ueda Bin, things like haiku flavor and humor are passive in character, the music of a nation’s ruin. Trust Ueda to put it so neatly and to the point. Just imagine actually performing such nonsense; you would only be laughed at by Ueda Bin himself. To begin with, is this thing you have written a play, or is it mere farce and foolery? Is it not so excessively passive that one cannot make head or tail of it? Forgive me for saying so, Kangetsu, but you would do better to polish your glass balls in the laboratory; even if you wrote a hundred or two hundred haiku-dramas, this music of national ruin simply will not do.”

paragraphs.source_en: Kangetsu, looking somewhat indignant, said, “Is it really so passive? I myself meant it to be quite active.” He began defending a matter that, in truth, made no difference whether one called it passive or active. “Take Kyoshi, for example. When Master Kyoshi composes the line, ‘Ah, the crow / Enraptured by the woman / Bathing below,’ I regard his making the crow fall in love with the woman as something highly active.”
